Liza Catan

Liza Catan

27 Highdown Road, Hove BN3 6ED. [lizacatan@googlemail.com]

Liza Catan  

claustro-agoraphobia, destructive narcissism, claustrum, psycho-somatic states of mind, enactment, Rey

This paper aims to illustrate Henri Rey's notion of the claustro-agoraphobic ‘syndrome’. Two case studies focus on beginning (entering into) and leaving (coming out from) treatment since claustro-agoraphobic anxieties tend to erupt with particular violence and clarity around these events, emerging in the transference and countertransference as struggles to settle and contain the patient in treatment. This process re-evokes the patient's lifelong struggle with a merged maternal object as they are alternately overwhelmed by fears of being entrapped or entombed, their individuality threatened, or by fears of abandonment and disintegration. Caught between alternating terrors, survival becomes the overriding preoccupation around which they evolve the characteristic defences of a liminal existence, disabling the therapist and resorting to flight as a last-ditch solution. In the final section, post-Kleinian theories of destructive narcissism are used to throw light on the interlinked psychic processes underlying Rey's claustro-agoraphobic syndrome.

Rosie Parker 1945-2010

Margot Waddell

Margot Waddell

British Psychoanalytical Society, Tavistock Clinic

Margot Waddell  

Over the decades that Rosie Parker and I were friends, we shared many joys and sorrows and political, cultural and personal tumult. Those were exciting, even heady decades and they brought with them both love and loss. But although initially having taken distinct paths - Rosie into feminist art history and I into child psychotherapy and latterly psychoanalysis - it was only in the second of those decades, from 1987 onwards, when Rosie trained and worked as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist, that the specificity of one of the central lynchpins of the relationship really emerged. Rosie's clinical work and writing became her main professional preoccupation for the rest of her life. She was able, in so mature and creative a way, to bring to her work not just a deeply felt clinical commitment, but also a freshness and depth derived from her distinguished accomplishments in other areas of life. Creative patients, in particular, encountered in Rosie a very special receptive ear, one finely attuned to the many registers of the artistic personality

Aside from the personal bonds - particularly around being mothers, having children and pursuing multiple friendships - we learned the meaning of true collaboration. This took three forms: that of confidential discussion of difficult clinical situations; that of supervision and referral; and that of our respective writing, in terms of literary and theoretical perspectives.

In relation to the referrals I made to her over time, I was absolutely confident not only about her clinical expertise, intuitive subtlety and soundness of practice, but also about the need, in each such case, for a particular quality of being, for an unusually deep, creative and aesthetic appreciation of the dynamics of the therapeutic relationship. When she became ill I saw some of these patients for consultation and each time my anticipation of the rich and what, more than once, was described as ‘life-saving’ work was confirmed. But it was the collaborative writing that became so significant a shared project for the two of us. From Torn in Two (Parker, 1995) onwards, neither of us wrote anything professionally that had not been thoroughly scrutinized and discussed by the other.

Tradition, Psychoanalysis and the Therapeutic Community

John Gale and Beatriz Sanchez

Beatriz Sanchez

24/5-6 The Coda Centre, 189 Munster Road, London SW6 6AW. [jg@cht.org.uk]

Holybourne Avenue, London SW15 4JL. [bs.surreal@gmail.com]

Beatriz Sanchez  

tradition, therapeutic community, Lacan, Gadamer, full speech, intersubjectivity

This paper addresses fundamental aspects of the notion of tradition in order to try to understand the foundations of the therapeutic community by drawing on the philosophy of Hans-Georg Gadamer and the psychoanalytic thought of Jacques Lacan. The authors argue that, although a Kleinian reading of the therapeutic community has been dominant, a hermeneutic approach can enrich our understanding through its emphasis on language, community and dwelling. This leads to a discussion - with the use of case examples drawn from the authors' work in therapeutic communities for the severely mentally ill - of memory, community and remembering, full speech, and the intersubjective nature of being (Heidegger's Mitsein) which situates us not just within tradition but within a specific set of tradition.

Diana Birkett  

It is often refreshing for English-speaking readers, if intimidating, to read papers on a familiar subject seen from a European perspective: there is a poetic quality to some of the writing that can bring to life a concept that has become tired and over-familiar. Here is an example from the Introduction (p. xx): ‘An inheritance of suffering, a sediment, a deposit of death that impairs their mental soundness, blurs their feelings and colonizes their internal world; a disturbing polysemy …’, even if this last word has us turning to the dictionary.

This excellent book is based on the work of the ongoing workshop of the European Federation for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, and the contributors all work with victims of state violence and torture in different parts of the world: Denmark, UK, South America, Israel, France, South Africa and Italy. They make reference to authors previously unknown to me, and it is therefore all the more frustrating that many quotations are followed by ‘(date needed)’, as the volume could benefit from further proof-reading.

The ordinariness of the title, Bearing Witness, in relation to the literature of trauma hides a challenge to traditional psychoanalytic thinking, though this is not a new one, with the claim that working with trauma is now at the cutting edge of psychoanalytic practice. There is the occasional homage to Freud, as in the final chapter by Dr Gautier, in which he recounts Freud's encounter with the hotel waitress, Katharina, when walking in the mountains on vacation, as the prototype of non-interpretative ‘bearing witness’; but the theme running through the book is that psychoanalytic neutrality is no longer appropriate in situations where state violence is involved: ‘In this situation, the psychoanalyst becomes a possible fellow-combatant in the struggle against barbarism’ (p. 158). The notion of a ‘testimonial pact’ between listener and speaker is explored: ‘If one considers psychoanalysis as an opportunity to take in and transform emotional and mental states, there can be no doubt that testimony is somehow linked to the psychoanalytic act of listening’ (Waintrater, 2004, p. 65). The aim is to help liberate the witness from the actual story, so that the object of the testimony is not what has been repressed: rather the manifest narrative unfolds in a way co-determined by the testimony receiver, who will refrain from any interpretative interruptions.

Elizabeth Ford  

Take the large words of the title of this book out of context for a moment and the scope of the enterprise feels dizzying - which might not be the frivolous response it appears, but a pointer to how ambitious a project this book is and that it will make demands. The book's epigraph should be noted as a warning: ‘Einstein said: “The only reason for time is so that everything doesn't happen at once”’. This deceptively simple statement leaves you puzzling over the questions it raises, and the complexities and mysteries implicit in the title. Fortunately, Rosine Jozef Perelberg is generous with her explanations, as well as a meticulous guide through Freudian metapsychology and, specifically here, his conception of psychic space and time.

At the outset the author makes clear her belief that psychoanalysis has made a revolutionary contribution to ‘the modern understanding of time and space in the constitution of the individual’ (p. 3). Mystics and poets have always expressed the difficulties which time and space present and how intense the longing for an escape from them can be. Is it not an attempt to resolve the intractable when Blake writes: ‘To see a World in a Grain of Sand/And a Heaven in a Wild Flower,/ Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand/And Eternity in an hour’ (Blake, 1988)? Or Crashaw's ‘Welcome, all wonders in one sight! Eternity shut in a span’? (Crashaw, 1973). Such ideas seem to speak to the wish for time and space to cease because they cause human beings to suffer, they deny them satisfaction.

In taking on time, space and phantasy, Perelberg is bringing into focus the nexus of concepts underpinning Freudian thinking as she grapples with complex and elusive processes of mind. For all the abstractions of the title, the book is of course rooted in clinical practice so, once the intricacies of theory have been unpacked, there are several chapters presenting this psychoanalytic understanding in action in the consulting room. Perelberg comes well equipped for the undertaking. Her academic training began in social anthropology. She possesses a deep knowledge of Freudian texts and, as she is steeped in both the French and the British analytic traditions, she brings a rich mixture of thinking, deeply absorbed and digested through both study and clinical work.
